game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
Much less a game than an interactive story. It's a slim game with few objectives and a lot of fluff around it. The game tends to cram exposition into everything, and doesn't allow you to skip or fast-forward any of it. Utimately, while the plot is about making a god of machines, it doesn't justify its deus ex machina storytelling.

[h1]Show, Don't Tell[/h1]
I do not know who's idea it was to not allow the player to fast-forward or skip dialogue, but it was a [b]terrible[/b] decision. The sheer amount of exposition and meaningless chatter in the game is astounding. And this isn't a once or twice occurance, it's a regularly reoccuring situation where key bits of info required to advance the plot sit behind a 4 or 5 minute long unskippable dialogue sequence. And that 10+ minute bit right before the end of the game, who thought that was a good idea? And does the "administrator" need to say something every time I upload a piece of relevant info? It's like having Clippy from MS Word permanently built into the game.

Furthermore, the level of hand-holding is ridiculous. First off, for a game about parsing and collecting information, there's very little you actually have to read. The game essentially takes a big neon highlighter and highlights every single thing that might be of importance. Then, they go ahead and show you exactly where you might've missed a clue or hint. Secondly, the game has these "pivotal" moments where you have to decide which one of multiple conflicting statements is true, except that the system highlights conflicts before you even discover them. It's such a self-defeating mechanism. Imagine if the Sherlock novels had Watson discover a false clue and Sherlock responding "But Watson, that can't be the real clue cause I'm going to find the real clue on page 86!"

And if the story was entralling, and the world-building was coherent, maybe those bad gameplay elements could be overlooked. But they aren't. The plot is cheesy and the writing is lazy. How many times do you plan on having a random character with no background conveniently appear to tie-up some loose ends and then disappear forever? It's honestly kind of amazing how a game where everything you do is character building manages to have some of the most one-dimensional characters I've ever seen.

[h1]Breakdown[/h1]
[b]Pros[/b]
[olist]
    [*][b]Chapter Select:[/b] Thanks for at least not making me have to replay the whole game to get an achievement.
[/olist]
[b]Cons[/b]
[olist]
    [*][b]Don't stop users from fast-forwarding text.[/b]
    [*][b]Narrative, not Narrate:[/b] I should be able to tell when I come across an important piece of dialogue. I don't need the game to highlight it a bright color, the music to change to be all dramatic, and Clippy at the top exclaiming, "Wow! That piece of dialogue sure seems important!" *wink* *wink* *nudge* *nudge*
[/olist]
[b]Score[/b]: 2/10

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[quote][url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/7871885/]Follow our curator page:[b] OCG-Curations[/b] if you like and want to see more reviews like this one.[/url][/quote]

[h1]Overview:[/h1]
Orwell takes place in a distopian near future in the fictional city of Bonton in The Nation. Orwell is the codename of a vastly advanced surveilance system. They outsource investigations to outsiders of the nation - you! It is your task to spy on suspects and inform the government of what is going on. Basically, you roleplay as "Mr. FBI Man".

[h1]The Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b]Interesting Story[/b] - The game is divided into five chapters, each representing a day in game. I won't be spoiling anything here so there isn't much to say, but I will state my overall impression. The story is good! If you take everything at face value you'll be in for a surprise when you realise this game is not as shallow as it may seem. Each chapter unveils another layer of mystery. There are also three endings (more on that later).

[*][b]Some Replayability[/b] - Every chapter has a few endings (usually two or three). After you finish the game, you may choose to replay starting from any chapter (subsequent ones are erased). Most unique paths you can take are linked to an achievement, so 100%-ing the game is pretty much just exploring every possibility. Don't get too exited though, as that took me about 8 hours and two playthroughs (but in the second one I did consult a guide to save time).

[*][b]Clean UI[/b] - I really like the clean, very intuitive interface. Which is good, considering as this UI is basically the whole game itself. The only downside is that it does not have a dark mode for playing at night, but it's not a dealbreaker.
[/list]

[h1]The Cons:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b]Hand Holding[/b] - You give information to Orwell by drag and dropping data chunks from your spy browser to the Orwell app. They are automatically outlined for you, which seems stupid, but it's a necesarry evil if you think about the programmers. However, one thing I don't like are the special chunks - the conflicts are highlighted in yellow, even if you didn't find both. This makes you extra careful before uploading as one makes the other invalid. This is how the story branches, but if you think about it it's a little stupid. How does the browser know about the conflict if you didn't access the other data chunk yet? This should be up to you - the "detective" to figure out. I wish they were all blue all the time, or turn yellow only after discovering both.

[*][b]Choices Almost Don't Matter[/b] - Remember when I said chapters? Well... they're pretty much isolated instances. Outcomes are mentioned from one to another, but only through slight dialogue changes. But the story progresses the same no matter what you do, until you reach chapter five and finally get to choose an ending.
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
Orwell is a good game because it explores an interesting concept and offers a good story to boot. While it's not as mindbending as I first expected, I still recommended it as a very interactive visual novel. If the topic interests you and don't mind the short playtime, this is a good game to pick up.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw: It took me a bit to get into this game, and some of the interface was confusing at first, but then I really got into it and enjoyed it a lot. The music and sound effects are subtle except when there's a stinger to get your attention, the UI is clean and snappy, the graphics style is pleasing to look at, and the story has a lot of depth and nuance. It's the sort of game that would've been great for my lineup of edutainment games as a teen when I was homeschooling, because of the amount of critical thinking and ethical choice involved. I don't think there's any way to fail a chapter, but I haven't tried inputting all the extraneous info that exists. That said, you WILL need a guide if you want to get all the achievements, and there are some good ones here on Steam. It took me about ten hours to 100%, which isn't bad for what is essentially a visual novel. My only complaint is that I wish the text advancement for things like phone conversations and especially that nearly ten minute call in the last chapter had an option to be even faster. I read quite fast, and especially on replays for achievements I found myself tabbing out and doing other things while letting the conversation roll in the background. That One Call in particular needs a way to skip through it; it was interesting the first time but not the second or third time. It'll take two to three runs of each chapter to get all the achievements.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You is a thought-provoking game that successfully delves into the complex world of surveillance and privacy, raising numerous ethical questions and dilemmas. Its core premise, which involves taking on the role of a government operative monitoring citizens' digital lives, is both innovative and unsettling. It challenges players to balance national security with personal privacy, making every decision carry significant weight and moral ambiguity.

Gameplay Mechanics

The mechanics are straightforward, primarily revolving around reading through documents, chat logs, and social media posts to piece together clues about potential threats. While this simplicity makes the game accessible, it can also lead to a repetitive and tedious experience. The process of sifting through information often lacks variety, and the gameplay can become monotonous over time. Moreover, the game's interface, although intuitive, sometimes suffers from minor bugs that can force you to reload the Game. There are also some minor instances where progression is unclear, leaving players uncertain about their next steps.

Narrative and Storytelling

One of the strengths of Orwell lies in its narrative, which includes several compelling plot twists that keep the player engaged. The story explores themes of power, trust, and the consequences of unchecked surveillance, offering moments of genuine intrigue and suspense. However, despite these high points, the overall plot can feel somewhat bland and unremarkable by the conclusion. The characters, while initially interesting, sometimes lack depth, and the story does not always capitalize on its potential to deliver a truly memorable experience.

Ethical Themes and Impact

Where Orwell truly shines is in its exploration of ethical issues. The game does not shy away from presenting the moral complexities of surveillance, forcing players to confront the impact of their actions on individuals' lives. This aspect of the game is its most compelling feature, prompting players to reflect on real-world implications and the delicate balance between security and privacy.

TLDR: 

Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You is a game with a powerful concept that effectively engages with important ethical themes. Its simple mechanics can become repetitive, and minor technical issues can hinder the experience. While the narrative has strong moments, it ultimately falls short of being truly remarkable. Nevertheless, the game’s exploration of surveillance and privacy makes it a worthwhile experience for those interested in thought-provoking and socially relevant games.

Pros:

- Engaging ethical themes and dilemmas
- Innovative and unsettling premise
- Compelling plot twists
- Intuitive interface

Cons:

- Repetitive and tedious mechanics
- Minor bugs and progression issues
- Overall bland and unremarkable plot
- Characters lack depth

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
An interesting title. It's essentially a simulation of what it would be like to work as an impartial agent for a foreign government, spying for them, gathering data and sharing it with your adviser so that they can make decisions about who is a suspect and attempt to stop them. This basically all takes place from your character's computer screen.

In essence, the plot revolves around you, the "investigator", being tasked with finding out who is responsible for a recent bombing in a public place within "The Nation" (the country that runs this Orwellian nightmare). The first chapter is basically the tutorial, but don't let that fool you into believing your choices don't matter.

EVERY piece of data you choose to share can be used by the "adviser" (a partner who can speak to and advise you but you can never speak to yourself) to make decisions about what to do next. If you, say, take words out of context, you can get someone arrested for nothing at all. Then again, maybe that's worth it (do the ends justify the means?) to stop a terrorist bombing. This game is basically a series of choices. You won't always have much time to act. Most of the time you're given free reign and only after tossing in specific information are you able to advance, but it works together pretty well. Once you beat the game, you're likely to want to replay chapters to fix details you messed up, causing an unexpected result. I often find I mess up more than once (I've played more than 6 hours, but I haven't seen every result) and, somewhat frustratingly, have to do the whole chapter over again just to get back to that point and fix it, but it's not so bad. If you approach the game as an "I'll try my best and live with the consequences" sort of thing, the end result could be pretty amazing. I highly recommend that at least for your first playthrough.

Don't fret over mistakes. Try your best.

And if you like the idea of being what basically amounts to a spy in the IT department, you'll probably enjoy this game. The sequel isn't quite as incredible, but that's mostly because it isn't really a sequel. I think it takes part along the same story which doesn't make much sense because I always got the impression you were the only team using Orwell. I think the developers just wanted to make another game and couldn't justify it properly. It's alright. I would still suggest playing the sequel after just because it's a fun concept and the developers deserve the support. They worked hard on this and it very clearly shows. Good concept, good aesthetic design, interesting story. It's a mystery you can unravel for yourself and it's a damn enjoyable one at that. Please, sincerely, give it a try if this sounds at all enticing.

It's not an immensely long game (probably about 6 hours for your first time through), but that by no means makes it less worthwhile.

It doesn't overstay its welcome and delivers a satisfying experience.

It's essentially a simulation of what it would be like to work as an impartial agent for a foreign government, spying for them, gathering data and sharing it with your adviser so that they can make decisions about who is a suspect and attempt to stop them. This basically all takes place from your character's computer screen. In essence, the plot revolves around you, the "investigator", being tasked with finding out who is responsible for a recent bombing in a public place within "The Nation" (the country that runs this Orwellian nightmare). The first chapter is basically the tutorial, but don't let that fool you into believing your choices don't matter. EVERY piece of data you choose to share can be used by the "adviser" (a partner who can speak to and advise you but you can never speak to yourself) to make decisions about what to do next. If you, say, take words out of context, you can get someone arrested for nothing at all. Then again, maybe that's worth it (do the ends justify the means?) to stop a terrorist bombing. This game is basically a series of choices. You won't always have much time to act. Most of the time you're given free reign and only after tossing in specific information are you able to advance, but it works together pretty well. Once you beat the game, you're likely to want to replay chapters to fix details you messed up, causing an unexpected result. I often find I mess up more than once (I've played more than 6 hours, but I haven't seen every result) and, somewhat frustratingly, have to do the whole chapter over again just to get back to that point and fix it, but it's not so bad. If you approach the game as an "I'll try my best and live with the consequences" sort of thing, the end result could be pretty amazing. I highly recommend that at least for your first playthrough. Don't fret over mistakes. Try your best. And if you like the idea of being what basically amounts to a spy in the IT department, you'll probably enjoy this game. The sequel isn't quite as incredible, but that's mostly because it isn't really a sequel. I think it takes part along the same story which doesn't make much sense because I always got the impression you were the only team using Orwell. I think the developers just wanted to make another game and couldn't justify it properly. It's alright. I would still suggest playing the sequel after just because it's a fun concept and the developers deserve the support. They worked hard on this and it very clearly shows. Good concept, good aesthetic design, interesting story. It's a mystery you can unravel for yourself and it's a damn enjoyable one at that. Please, sincerely, give it a try if this sounds at all enticing. It's not an immensely long game (probably about 6 hours for your first time through), but that by no means makes it less worthwhile. It doesn't overstay its welcome and delivers a satisfying experience.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I must say I never heard from that game, after it pops up on Steam at its release date.

And I'm suprised to say, that this game catched me aloen by its name!

I awaited a Big Brother game ... and I got a Big Brother game ... a game, where you can be Big Brother yourself.

You take control of a new surveilance system called Orwell to find the people responsible for a terror bombing.
Fot that you can check websites, 'listen' to calls and chats and search through phones and computers.

Pros:
- Easy to learn gameplay
- Fitting graphic style and background music
- Good story
- 'Just one more minute/level/stage'
- Different endings and outcomes of story parts

Neutral:
- 4-6 hour for a single walkthrough
- Balanced 'Cliché' and 'Suprised' moments/characters

Cons:
- A bit to simple gameplay (there are only some situations, where it is a bit hard to decide between different choices)
- No 'dead ends'
- Linear story progress

As this game offers its first (of five) episodes for free as a demo (works also as a tutorial), you can easily test out, if you like its gameplay. The initial price of around 10 € is very fair, so do the devs a favor if you like the demo and buy it directly. ;)

I really hope the devs use the base concept/gameplay for some more games! I really like that detective style of conecting clues. But at the same time I hope they expend the concept with video footage to analyze, dead ends, more conflicting clues.
